newsitem.title: UK: Mideast tankers steady, W. Africa VLCCs edge up.
newsitem.headline: Mideast tankers steady, W. Africa VLCCs edge up.

text.p: Rates for very large crude carriers (VLCCs) from the Middle East ended the week little changed while from West Africa they showed signs of firming on good enquiry, brokers said.

At least two West Africa/U.S. Gulf VLCCs were heard fixed at W67.5, up from W65 on Thursday. "Activity on 90,000 tonners is coming down. People are taking VLCCs out of West Africa in preference and that is pushing them up," one broker said.
VLCCs from the North Sea to the U.S. also edged up to W65 from W60 on good enquiry. "I can see interest in North Sea/USAC growing next week and rates firming a bit more," another broker said.

Middle East VLCC rates were flat after an uneventful week, with rates westwards at W60, to Japan at W65 and to Singapore at W50. Unusually, no ultra-large crude carriers were reported fixed over the last week.

Brokers E.A. Gibson said said Middle East VLCCs totalled a steady 15 vessels with just under four million tonnes fixed, and predicted that 57 ships of 17.2 million tonnes would be available over the next four weeks.
Brokers Galbraith's Ltd said that despite the Chinese new year, rates for modern tonnage on Mideast/East voyages could edge up, with the gap between old and new ships continuing to widen.
However, ships that have been left in the first 20 days of February "might have to take below 'last done' to get moving," they added.

Activity in the inter-U.K./Cont sector was moderate "but not enough to push rates up," one broker said. He said 80,000 tonners were continuing to fall, hitting W95 on Friday, almost 10 points down on the week, and he expected rates to decline further next week.
Cross-Med rates were steady, with 80,000 tonners at W130 and 130,000 tonne ships at W92.5, an Italian broker said.
Fuel oil was also little changed, with 25,000 tonnes inter-U.K./Cont at W210 and cross-Med at W195.

In the U.S., 70,000 tonne crude cargoes continued to fall to W130, down some 20 points on the week. "It's just a matter of not enough cargoes, too many ships," a U.S. broker said. Fuel oil was quiet, with 50,000 tonnes still notionally around W165.
